The E sub-score for Team II, with two adaptors, was 17 which is close to the mean of 18,
thus leaning toward preferring an efficiency in regard to detail. At the same time, Team I,
all innovators, with an R score of 25, indicated less adherence to efficiency of detail. Both
team leaders noticed that the innovative students reported less note-taking and were more
inclined to “brainstorm” topics or use nonlinear processes.
c onformity and c onsensus
The Team II leader also reported several instances in the area of conformity and consen-
sus. The adaptive team member was more concerned about their team moving forward
together and/or getting along, and they expressed the most frustration when this did not
happen. The innovative student team member was more likely to work individually at first,
bringing their results back to the team later for discussion; whereas the adaptive student
tended to work with the full group. Again these results are also indicated by the R sub-
factor performance scores for the two teams. Team I with a score of 45 above the mean of
36 indicated a preference to “think out of the box.” Whereas Team II with a score of 37.3
tended to prefer group work rather than to work individually. On both teams the Innova-
tive students were perceived as being abrasive and occasionally even offensive in word
and/or action. The adaptive member on Team II was perceived as offensive due to their
“condescending” attitudes and tendency to reject the ideas of the innovator student team
member. This last tendency included one team informant, as related by the team members
to the teacher privately, and with one other individual adaptive student as reported by their
team informant.
r elevance
Both teams had issues surrounding the perceived relevance of the input from their innova-
tive team members. Adaptive team members did not always see value in the ideas of their
innovative teammates. One Innovative teammate felt that their work was disregarded and/
or omitted with no good excuse.
c onflict
Team I was composed all innovators. Team II was composed of one innovator and two
adaptive members. Team II experienced the greatest amount of conflict overall, as
reported by the team informants. The conflict, on Team II, as stated earlier, is related to
a composition of adaptors and innovators whereas Team I was composed of all innovators.
It would have been interesting to have assigned the Team I leader as the Team II leader.
This assignment would have made the Kirton A-I Inventory Performance scores on Team
II have a 40 point range, which might have led to team disruption and major conflict
[Kirton, M. J., 1994].

In general the students expressed appreciation of each other’s work by the end of the semes-

chunks.content:
ter. Adaptive members seem to recognize value in the innovative teammates bringing ideas
to the table, ideas which they might not have devised on their own.
c onclusion
This preliminary study, in spite of small sample size, has demonstrated that applying cog-
nitive style theory to characterize and better understand the personal dynamics of stu-
dents working in teams is both useful and appropriate. Analysis of the data in this study
indicates that their exist relationships between cognitive styles and student’s team project
behaviors, but further and more rigorous investigations must be made relative to this
hypothesis.
A major application of the Kirton A-I performance scores is apparent from the observed
student behaviors in this study. In the future the author will not only utilize major, GPA, and
professional experience to develop project teams, but Kirton A-I performance scores will be
incorporated into the assignment process. The Kirton A-I performance scores will be used to
form groups with either homogeneous or heterogeneous cognitive styles for group activities.

An e thnographic s tudy of M sis s tudent e-l earning c ultures
Project: An ethnographic study designed to investigate remote learning enhancements
in the context of a graduate database class at the University of Mary Hardin-Baylor. The

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ABSTRACT
chunks.content:
emphasis of the study is to gain an understanding of the e-learning culture of the graduate
MSIS student body at UMHB. All results would maintain anonymity.
The Group: The graduate students in the MSIS degree program are required to have either
an undergraduate degree in Information Systems or an undergraduate degree in another
major with adequate relevant work experience. The current class, Database Development
and Administration, has eight students enrolled. I suspect that student preference for class
environments swings from totally online to only in a traditional classroom environment. Sim-
ilarly, I suspect that the student backgrounds vary from having taken only traditional classes
to a desire to take only Internet-based courses.
The Request: As a term project team leader, I am requesting that you serve as a concealed
observer of your team members. With your help we will complete an observation of their
behaviors and the values and beliefs causing these behaviors.
Background: There are two kinds of cultures: objective and subjective culture. We are
interested in discovering both types of culture present on your team. The visible part of
culture is the objective part. It includes: eye contact, greetings, initiative, food, clothing,
and time consciousness. Objective culture is supported by the subjective culture. This is the
internal part of culture that drives or motivates the visible, objective culture. It consists of
motivations, beliefs, and worldview.
Methodology: Gather data through observation which might be categorized by the follow-
ing list of things to look for in the individual under observation. Next week I will interview
you in order to submit a written report on each of your team member observations. This
information will be kept just between you and me to preserve confidentially.
Think of the adjectives which describe the typical business person. Here is a list that comes
to my mind: hard driving, self-confident, self-reliant, tough negotiator, decisive, fair, moti-
vated, fact-based, and unemotional, uncaring, scientific, unfeeling, well-educated, rational,
closed, control.
Now think of the adjectives describing positive relationships between team members: trust-
ing, caring, emotional, friendship, win-win, self-expression, comfort, and exposed.
But for the negative relationships between team members we might have: vague, dependent,
unknown.
In some cases as the leader you could possibly be asking a person to neglect/ignore every-
thing they have been taught all of their life, to give up control, and to open themselves up
to potential misfortune or failure based on feelings.
